Meeting Header:
Date: 2028-10-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Derek Huang (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CSM), Anya Lopez (CTO - Sierra), Ravi Menon (Head of MLOps), Claire Duval (Lead SRE), Owen Park (Product)

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Reviewed week-over-week benchmark numbers: p50/p95 latency + sustained throughput vs Sierra's incumbent (CloudForge).
- Discussed routing/fallback playbook adjustments and next stress windows.
- Agreed Redwood shows lower p50 and better tail under batching but unit-cost tradeoffs matter.

Topics: latency delta, throughput stability, routing playbook, on-prem/VPC concerns, security docs

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Alright folks, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick 45ish minute run through, goal is walk the bench results we ran last night and nail down the routing/fallback next steps. First time check, is everyone good on audio?
[00:12] Anya: Yep, all good here.
[00:15] Ravi: Good to go.
[00:18] Derek: Great, I'll share my screen in a sec with the dashboards — trying to keep it high level then deep-dive where you want.
[00:22] Maya: Derek, maybe start with the headline numbers vs CloudForge, then we can jump into the oddities.
[00:27] Derek: Sure. So quick snapshot — p50 for our tuned LLM route at 128-token payload is ~82 ms, p95 at 320 ms. CloudForge reported p50 ~120 ms and p95 ~410 ms on their public numbers for the same workload. Sustained throughput in our lab with continuous batching (batch size ~8, async NVLink) was 110 rps, with 10% variance over 30 minutes; CloudForge baseline showed 75 rps in their published tests.
[01:05] Claire: Can I ask how you're measuring p95? Is that including network hop to the VPC egress? Because our staging runs remove some of that, I want apples-to-apples.
[01:15] Derek: Good call. The numbers I just quoted are server-side from the inference container — so excludes customer-side network. For the staging harness you ran earlier this week, we have the end-to-end numbers: end-to-end p50 ~120 ms, p95 ~430 ms which is comparable to CloudForge's E2E reported. The server-side delta is where we show gains due to kernel selection and kv-cache reuse.
[01:35] Ravi: That matches what we saw last night — inc lived test: CloudForge p95 spiked during burst windows. Our concern is tail under real traffic — how consistent is your fallback?
[01:45] Derek: Right, fallback is two-tier: first route to a lower-cost quantized variant we keep warm (q4 or q8 depending on perf profile), if that still breaches latency SLO we route to a smaller model with guaranteed <600 ms SLO. We also have a timeout-based circuit-breaker to avoid queue pileups.
[02:03] Owen: How much of a quality delta do we expect with q4 vs your base model? Our product team worried about hallucination increases.
[02:11] Derek: In our evals, q4 caused a ~1.5 point drop on our prompt-set BLEU-like metric for your typical prompts, and ~2% higher rate of short hallucinations. For customer UI, we recommend fallback only for non-critical routes or after a retry with an expanded prompt context.
[02:31] Anya: Can the quantized variant be used as primary for lower-cost flows? We have a batch of low-priority queries that could accept that.
[02:38] Maya: Yes, absolutely. You can tag routes as best-effort and they'll hit the quantized pool. That is a common play to save unit cost. We'll include a suggested routing config.
[02:47] Claire: About the burst windows — last night's log showed a 30% CPU steal on the host at 02:12 UTC, any idea why?
[02:54] Derek: We saw a scheduler jitter on the orchestration node — likely due to the autoscaler resizing a different node pool. We pushed a kernel-level pin for the inference container in the lab run which reduced jitter; in prod we recommend dedicated capacity slots if you need strict jitter bounds.
[03:15] Ravi: Dedicated capacity is interesting but what's the delta on cost? Our finance will object if it's a 3x increase.
[03:22] Maya: We'll run a cost delta sheet — but from prior pilots, dedicated reserved slots tend to increase baseline but reduce variance; net unit cost can be neutral if you maintain utilization. We'll send a modeled example for your traffic profile.
[03:35] Owen: Is there an easy way to simulate the exact traffic pattern we saw in production — like the 90s burst then steady?
[03:41] Derek: Yes, we can generate a traffic replay harness with your traces and run it against both hosted and dedicated configs. That's actually one of the action items to prove tail behavior.
[03:50] Anya: Okay great. Can we talk about the one weird run where p95 was higher than expected even though p50 stayed low? That was 01:12 UTC in the logs.
[03:59] Derek: I have that open — at 01:12 we had a cache miss storm because the prefix-based kv cache warmed up slower; there were many unique long prefixes in that window. So the batcher got suboptimal packing and latency spiked.
[04:17] Claire: How do we mitigate cache miss storms? We need predictable tails.
[04:21] Derek: A few levers: increase KV cache memory allocation (we tried +20% in the test which reduced p95 by ~35 ms), enable per-route warmup (prepopulate common prefixes), and tighten batching timeout to avoid sending partial micro-batches. There are tradeoffs: smaller batches lower throughput and raise unit cost.
[04:40] Ravi: What about routing to an isolated warm pool during predicted high-unique-prefix periods?
[04:44] Derek: Yep that's the routing carveout pattern we suggested: on anomaly detection, route to a dedicated warm pool with warmed kv-cache and smaller batch windows. It reduces p95 but costs more during the carveout.
[04:56] Anya: Let's talk concrete numbers — in the test where you increased cache +20% what were the p50/p95 and throughput?
[05:02] Derek: With +20% KV memory and tighter batching (timeout 6ms), we saw server-side p50 88 ms, p95 290 ms, throughput 95 rps sustained (down from 110 rps). That's compared to the baseline run (no +kv): p50 82 ms, p95 320 ms, throughput 110 rps. So you trade some throughput for tail stability.
[05:26] Owen: And how did CloudForge behave with the same cache bump?
[05:29] Derek: CloudForge's architecture doesn't expose kv cache tuning in the same way; with our replay of their public config we couldn't reduce their tail as effectively. Their p95 still hovered ~380-420 ms under similar load.
[05:42] Claire: Security question — if we route to a quantized pool or smaller model, does the data leave the VPC or any different ingress path?
[05:49] Maya: No, for Private or Dedicated the traffic stays within the VPC. For Hosted, we support VPC peering and private egress options; nothing is sent to third-party. We'll annotate the routing playbook with data path details.
[06:02] Ravi: Great. One more ask — can Redwood export request-level traces that map token times so we can correlate spikes?
[06:10] Derek: Yes, we can produce per-request token timing traces; they're a bit verbose but we can sample at 1% and give you a full endpoint for debug.
[06:18] Anya: That would help.
[06:20] Maya: Let's surface the next steps — I think we have four technical experiments: 1) staging stress window with replay (Ravi), 2) Derek to share tuned flags and kernel list, 3) Redwood to send routing playbook and cost delta, 4) Claire to share security contacts. Anything else?
[06:33] Owen: Can we also get a short write-up on failure modes — like cache miss storms and autoscaler jitter — so our infra team can digest quickly?
[06:39] Derek: Yep, I'll draft a 1-pager and include mitigations.
[06:42] Maya: Okay, schedule — sounds like we want the stress window early next week and meet again on 2028-10-09 for results and a canary plan?
[06:50] Anya: Works for us.
[06:52] Ravi: 10/9 is fine.
[06:54] Claire: Fine here.
[06:56] Maya: Cool. Quick last note, we noticed a path where if the quantized fallback is used too aggressively you can increase downstream cost due to retries; our recommended default is 1 retry to quantized, then escalate.
[07:10] Owen: Makes sense.
[07:12] Maya: Any questions before we close?
[07:15] Anya: No, thanks team.
[07:17] Derek: I'll upload the kernel flags and a short playbook to the shared folder after the call.
[07:21] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the items and the 10/9 invite. Bye.

End of transcript.
